upsert.center: University of Liverpool Small Animal Teaching Hospital
upsert.status: Current translational canine clinical trial
upsert.contacts: Prof. Tim Bentley — Tim.Bentley@liverpool.ac.uk; Small Animal Teaching Hospital — sath@liverpool.ac.uk
upsert.notes: University of Liverpool identifies DOG-FIGhT as Professor Bentley's current translational canine clinical trial. upsert.title: BIOCERA-VET injectable bone cement for canine appendicular osteosarcoma
upsert.location: Oniris Veterinary Teaching Hospital, Nantes, France
upsert.status: Recruiting
upsert.intervention: Minimally invasive percutaneous injection of BIOCERA-VET calcium-phosphate bone cement into the osteosarcoma-affected bone under fluoroscopic guidance; limb-preserving palliative treatment.
upsert.eligibility_summary: Large- or giant-breed dogs with appendicular osteosarcoma diagnosed by imaging; bone biopsy may be performed if diagnosis is uncertain.
upsert.notes: Primary Oniris page explicitly states recruitment is currently open and describes a prospective multicenter clinical study with TheraVet. Initial protocol visit is covered. Treatment is palliative but directly treats/stabilizes the tumor-bearing bone and is therefore included under the treatment-focused scope.

upsert.contacts: AniCura AOI — aoi@anicura.ch; +41 (0)41 783 07 77
upsert.funding: Confirm study-covered and owner-paid costs directly with AniCura AOI.
upsert.notes: Current AniCura AOI page states that dogs with superficial tumors are treated in a clinical study with intralesional special immunocytokines in collaboration with ETH Zürich. ETH research material describes canine F8/L19 immunocytokines and an initiated small clinical trial in dog patients with superficial tumors. upsert.title: FLASH radiotherapy for canine superficial malignant tumors
upsert.center: University Hospital for Companion Animals, University of Copenhagen / Lund University
upsert.status: Recruiting/current project — University of Copenhagen lists patients for the 2020–2027 FLASH radiotherapy project
upsert.contacts: Betina Børresen — bb@sund.ku.dk
upsert.funding: The project states that treatment and follow-up visits are paid by the project; owner is responsible for EU pet passport/rabies requirements for travel to Sweden.
upsert.notes: Dogs with a cancer mass in skin, subcutis or oral cavity, including incompletely removed/residual tumor, may participate when there is expected therapeutic benefit. Dogs receive 1–4 radiotherapy treatments over up to four weeks; most receive FLASH and a smaller group conventional radiotherapy. Treatment requires travel within the Copenhagen/Lund collaboration.

upsert.title: Fluorescence lifetime imaging to guide cancer surgery in dogs and cats
upsert.center: Ghent University Faculty of Veterinary Medicine
upsert.status: Recruiting — current Ghent University participation page invites dogs and cats scheduled for tumor surgery
upsert.contacts: Simone Janssen — simone.janssen@ugent.be; Prof. Hilde de Rooster — hilde.derooster@ugent.be; referrals: chirurgie.khd@ugent.be
upsert.funding: Project covers pathological assessment of the removed mass; Ghent states no additional costs compared with non-study surgical patients.
upsert.notes: Clinical study using intraoperative fluorescence lifetime imaging with indocyanine green to improve discrimination of tumor from non-tumor tissue and increase the chance of complete cancer removal during surgery. Dogs or cats with cancer already scheduled, or to be scheduled, for tumor resection may participate.

upsert.title: CARE trial: autophagy inhibition plus radiation for canine glioma
upsert.center: UC Davis Weill School of Veterinary Medicine / Translational Brain Tumor Center
upsert.status: Actively recruiting — UC Davis recruitment announcement published September 3, 2026
upsert.contacts: UC Davis Veterinary Center for Clinical Trials — (530) 754-1954; contact Dr. Christine Toedebusch / study team via the official UC Davis page
upsert.funding: Study covers all study procedures and provides $4,000 toward radiation therapy; owners remain responsible for radiation costs beyond the study contribution.
upsert.notes: Combined Autophagy inhibition and Radiation to improve Efficacy in canine glioma (CARE). Dogs receive an experimental IV autophagy-inhibiting drug twice weekly for four weeks concurrently with standard radiation therapy, with brain-tumor biopsy before and after treatment. Current UC Davis materials state dogs with MRI-suspected glioma may be screened; final eligibility is determined by the neuro-oncology team.

upsert.title: Quasiorganelle therapy for canine histiocytic sarcoma
upsert.center: Michigan State University Veterinary Medical Center
upsert.status: Actively recruiting — current MSU clinical-trials page and August 24, 2026 recruitment announcement
upsert.contacts: MSU Medical Oncology Team — (517) 353-5420; cvm.oncoinfo@msu.edu
upsert.funding: Funded trial. Trial-associated tests, quasiorganelle treatment, hospitalization, blood/fecal sampling, imaging and treatment of trial-related complications are covered after enrollment; initial evaluation is charged.
upsert.notes: First cohort receives weakened non-disease-causing Listeria-derived quasiorganelle therapy alone; second cohort receives quasiorganelle therapy including gene therapy. Up to 5 visible lesions are allowed with summed longest dimensions under 15 cm. Weekly treatment x4, then 2 weeks off, repeated for a total 16-week treatment period. While enrolled, dogs should not live with someone pregnant or planning pregnancy.

upsert.title: PRISM: radiation-treatment access and funded follow-up for canine glioma
upsert.center: UC Davis Weill School of Veterinary Medicine / Translational Brain Tumor Center
upsert.status: Actively recruiting — UC Davis recruitment announcement published September 3, 2026
upsert.contacts: UC Davis Veterinary Center for Clinical Trials — (530) 754-1954; contact Dr. Christine Toedebusch / PRISM study team via the official UC Davis page
upsert.funding: Radiation pathway provides $3,000 toward radiation treatment and covers trial-related follow-up care, including follow-up visits and brain MRI examinations. The observational/palliative pathway instead provides $3,000 toward the initial diagnostic workup and covers trial-related follow-up care.
upsert.notes: OTHER TREATMENT-ACCESS OPPORTUNITY — not an experimental anticancer-treatment trial. PRISM is primarily a research/monitoring study. Dogs in its radiation pathway may receive standard radiation therapy according to the owner's wishes, with $3,000 study support toward radiation and funded trial-related follow-up. The study also has a non-treatment observational/palliative pathway.
